transcript:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: HelioBank x Redwood Inference — Security review (change management + audit logs)
Date: 2025-01-16
Time: 19:03 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees:
- Miguel Santos (Redwood Inference)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood Inference)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference)
- Paula Mendes (Redwood Inference)
- Priya Desai (HelioBank)
- Tom Wagner (HelioBank)
- Elena Morozova (HelioBank)
- Ben Carter (HelioBank)

Summary (auto-generated):
HelioBank reviewed Redwood’s change management controls for Dedicated capacity, focusing on staged rollouts, approval workflows, and audit log completeness. Redwood explained upcoming Dedicated staged rollouts (multi-stage traffic weights with metric gates), manual approvals, and fail-safe holds. HelioBank asked about audit event fields, retention, SIEM export, and RBAC separation between Redwood operators and customer admins.

Topics (auto-generated):
- Dedicated pool change management and staged rollouts
- Approval model and separation of duties
- Audit logs: event types, fields, retention, export/SIEM
- Failure modes: missing metrics, evaluator health, rollback behavior
- RBAC: roles, scopes, and customer access

Action items (auto-generated):
- Miguel Santos — Send HelioBank the rollout audit event examples and retention statement.
- Kevin Osei — Confirm SIEM export options (webhook/export pipeline) and typical delivery latency.
- Marcus Lin — Share RBAC matrix excerpt for rollout approve/abort permissions.
- Paula Mendes — Provide recommended defaults for gates and explanation of “pause vs rollback” policy.


Transcript

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Cool. Alright, folks, thanks for making the time. This is mainly a security and compliance review, change management, audit logs—stuff that’s coming up in your vendor questionnaire. Marcus and Kevin are here from Security and audit logging. Paula is product for rollout policies.

[00:15] Priya Desai: Great. Thanks, Miguel. Yeah, we’re trying to understand your change control posture, especially around model updates and runtime config changes on Dedicated. We’ve had some pain with other providers where we can’t tell who changed what, and approvals are… basically Slack messages.

[00:32] Tom Wagner: And for us, we need evidence. Like, actual audit events we can export, retain, and show to auditors. Not just “trust us.”

[00:41] Miguel Santos: Makes sense. Before we dive in, quick context check—this is for your planned Dedicated pool, correct? Not the shared hosted API.

[00:49] Elena Morozova: Correct. Dedicated reserved pool. We’ll be running in your managed cloud, but logically isolated, fixed capacity.

[00:56] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[01:00] Marcus Lin: And just to frame it: for Dedicated, we treat the pool and its serving configuration as change-managed assets. We’re building out more first-class rollout controls because the blast radius is real on reserved pools.

[01:12] Priya Desai: Yep, that’s exactly what we want to talk about.

[01:16] Ben Carter: And I’m here for procurement. I’ll probably be mostly quiet unless there’s something contractual.

[01:22] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[01:25] Priya Desai: So first, can you describe what “change management” means in your system? Like what constitutes a change? Model version, prompt templates, runtime parameters, autoscaling? Where does it start and end.

[01:39] Paula Mendes: Yeah. In our world, changes relevant to rollout controls include: model version pins, quantization profile changes, runtime flags that affect batching/caching, routing policies that alter traffic allocation, and pool-level capacity guardrail settings. Prompt changes are typically on your side unless you store prompts in Redwood, which most customers don’t.

[01:57] Elena Morozova: Right, we won’t store prompts in the vendor.

[02:00] Paula Mendes: For Dedicated staged rollouts—what we’re delivering—those changes get encapsulated in a RolloutPlan with stages. Each stage shifts a deterministic percentage of traffic to the new “target” configuration.

[02:13] Tom Wagner: Deterministic meaning… you can reproduce the split? Like same user always goes to the same side?

[02:19] Paula Mendes: Exactly. We use consistent hashing so that “5%” isn’t random per request. It’s stable assignment.

[02:27] Priya Desai: Ok. Now approvals. Do you support approvals for changes? And can we enforce separation of duties? Like one person proposes, another approves.

[02:36] Marcus Lin: We do. There are two layers: who can edit a rollout plan and who can advance stages / approve. For Dedicated, we can enforce that stage advancement requires a separate permission, and optionally a distinct role. We also log both the requestor and approver.

[02:54] Priya Desai: Is that available today or is it part of the staged rollout thing.

[02:58] Paula Mendes: The approvals concept exists in our general rollout framework, but what’s new in this project is making it first-class for Dedicated reserved pools, including per-stage approvals and gating.

[03:09] Miguel Santos: And to be transparent: in the “today” state, most Dedicated changes are executed as pool-level updates with a lot of manual process. The staged rollout system is what we’re rolling out to address exactly what you’re asking.

[03:22] Elena Morozova: That matches what we heard in the earlier demo. Ok.

[03:25] Tom Wagner: I’m going to be annoying and ask audit log specifics. When you say “we log,” what does that mean? Is it an immutable audit trail? What fields? Can it be exported to a SIEM? Retention?

[03:38] Kevin Osei: Not annoying at all. The audit log is append-only; events are generated by the control plane for security-relevant actions. For rollout actions, we emit events like: rollout.create, rollout.update, rollout.approval.granted, rollout.approval.denied, rollout.abort, rollout.auto_hold, and rollback actions when applicable.

[03:57] Priya Desai: You said “auto hold” — what triggers that.

[04:00] Paula Mendes: Gates failing. So, for example, if p95 latency exceeds a threshold, or 5xx error rate spikes, or queue depth crosses a limit, the evaluator will hold the rollout. It does not proceed. That hold event is audited.

[04:13] Elena Morozova: Is it auto rollback or auto hold?

[04:16] Paula Mendes: Defaults are generally hold first. Rollback can be configured but we’re cautious—rollbacks can also be disruptive on reserved capacity. We tend to require manual confirmation before rollback unless it’s a severe threshold.

[04:30] Tom Wagner: Great. Back to fields. What do I get in the event?

[04:34] Kevin Osei: Typical fields include: timestamp, actor identity (user or service), actor type, tenant_id, pool_id, rollout_plan_id, rollout_plan_version, stage_id, previous_stage_id, request_id, source_ip if it’s an interactive console or API call, and a “diff” reference. For updates we log the changed fields, not just “something changed.”

[04:58] Priya Desai: Changed fields as in before/after values?

[05:01] Kevin Osei: For many fields, yes. Some are redacted if they could contain secrets, but for rollout config it’s usually safe: weights, gate thresholds, evaluation windows, required approver roles, that kind of thing.

[05:14] Tom Wagner: Is this integrated with your SOC 2 controls? We have to map to CC7-ish change management and logging.

[05:22] Marcus Lin: Yes. Our audit events and retention are part of our SOC 2 program. The rollout changes are in scope because they can affect availability and security posture. We can provide a control mapping statement in the security package.

[05:36] Priya Desai: And export? We don’t want to log into a console to show an auditor.

[05:42] Kevin Osei: Two options typically. One, you can export audit logs via our audit log export pipeline—think S3-style bucket delivery in your account on a schedule. Two, for some customers we support streaming to SIEM via webhook or a partner integration. The exact method depends on environment and your preference.

[06:02] Ben Carter: Is SIEM streaming an add-on?

[06:05] Miguel Santos: It can be bundled depending on tier. We’ll follow up with what’s included in your package. We don’t need to decide that today.

[06:11] Priya Desai: Retention: what’s the default?

[06:14] Kevin Osei: Default is 400 days in our system for enterprise plans. Some customers require longer, and we handle that via export + your retention on your side. If you need, say, 7 years, we recommend exporting.

[06:30] Tom Wagner: Ok, so you keep about a year. That’s fine if we export.

[06:34] Elena Morozova: Let’s talk about approvals again. Do we control approvals, or is Redwood approving changes?

[06:41] Miguel Santos: Great question. For Dedicated, today a lot of changes are initiated by Redwood operators because we’re managing the pool. But for enterprise, we can scope controls so that your tenant admins can initiate rollouts for your pool, and your approvers can approve. Redwood can be excluded except for break-glass.

[06:59] Priya Desai: Break-glass meaning… your oncall can override?

[07:03] Marcus Lin: Yes, but it is controlled, audited, and limited to incident response. Break-glass actions are clearly marked in audit logs. And the permissions are separated.

[07:15] Tom Wagner: Do you support SSO? We don’t allow local accounts for privileged actions.

[07:20] Marcus Lin: SSO/SAML for console access, yes. And API tokens can be scoped. For stage approvals, it’s either via console with SSO, or via API with a token bound to an identity with the right permission.

[07:34] Elena Morozova: For API—do you have a concept of “service account” vs “human account”?

[07:39] Marcus Lin: Yes. We log whether it’s a user identity or service identity. And we encourage approvals to be human-only. You can enforce policy where stage advancement requires human approver, not a service.

[07:53] Priya Desai: That’s important. We’ve seen auto-advance in CI systems that basically bypasses review.

[08:00] Paula Mendes: Auto-advance can exist, but we’re building safeguards. Example: even with auto-advance enabled, if evaluator health is degraded or metrics are missing, we pause, not proceed.

[08:12] Elena Morozova: Metrics missing—can you elaborate? Like if Prometheus is down, what happens.

[08:18] Paula Mendes: Sure. Our gate evaluator queries our telemetry pipeline. If the window doesn’t have fresh enough datapoints—or if query latency is too high—we mark the gate evaluation “inconclusive” and the stage can’t advance. The system fails safe into hold.

[08:34] Priya Desai: Good. We would rather pause than push a bad change.

[08:38] Tom Wagner: But that does raise an audit question: do you log “we paused because metrics missing” distinctly from “gate failed.”

[08:46] Kevin Osei: Yes, those are different reasons. The hold event includes a reason code. For example: GATE_THRESHOLD_BREACH vs METRICS_STALE vs EVALUATOR_DEGRADED.

[08:59] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[09:01] Miguel Santos: I’ll also note: we’re dogfooding this internally on Redwood-managed pools first. We’re learning a lot about evaluator lag and missing metrics behavior.

[09:12] Elena Morozova: Evaluator lag? Like it doesn’t catch issues fast enough?

[09:16] Paula Mendes: Exactly. If the evaluator is running behind, we don’t want stage advancement to happen blindly. So we added a “stop-the-line” mode where if evaluator ticks are late, rollouts pause.

[09:29] Priya Desai: That’s actually a great example for our change management story—controls plus monitoring.

[09:35] Tom Wagner: Ok, now I want to understand the approval steps. Let’s say someone creates a rollout plan to update a model. What is the sequence.

[09:44] Paula Mendes: High level: create plan (draft), validate gates and capacity headroom rules, submit for execution, start stage 1 at a small weight, run evaluation window, if gates pass and approvals are satisfied, advance to the next stage. Each transition can require approval.

[10:05] Elena Morozova: And if it fails, you hold. Can you automatically revert traffic to previous stage weight.

[10:11] Paula Mendes: Yes, in many cases, holding means “stop increasing.” It can also set traffic back to the previous stable stage, depending on configuration. That’s part of the policy.

[10:22] Priya Desai: When you say “configuration,” can we set those policies ourselves.

[10:27] Miguel Santos: In beta, it’s mostly operator-driven with enterprise opt-in. But the direction is yes—customers with appropriate permissions will configure their rollout plans.

[10:39] Tom Wagner: Ok. So in beta, we might still rely on Redwood to set it up.

[10:43] Miguel Santos: Correct, but we’ll do it in collaboration and with explicit governance.

[10:48] Ben Carter: Sorry, what does “beta” timeline look like.

[10:52] Miguel Santos: We’re targeting a limited beta with 2–3 enterprise customers after internal dogfood. I can’t promise dates on this call, but it’s on the near-term roadmap. We can align it to your pilot window.

[11:05] Priya Desai: Our key requirement is: no unapproved changes to production. If Redwood needs to patch something, we need notification and an audit trail.

[11:14] Marcus Lin: Understood. Contractually we can commit to change notification windows for non-emergency changes. For emergency changes, we still act, but we document and audit them.

[11:26] Tom Wagner: Is notification via email? Ticket? API.

[11:30] Miguel Santos: Typically via email + status page + your Slack channel if you have one. But change events are also visible in console. There’s not currently an “audit event webhook” for notifications, but export can cover it after the fact.

[11:46] Elena Morozova: Ok. And does the audit log include “who at Redwood” did it.

[11:51] Kevin Osei: Yes, Redwood operator identity is captured. It’s not “system.” It’s a named user or service identity.

[11:58] Priya Desai: That’s key.

[12:01] Tom Wagner: Are audit logs tamper-proof.

[12:04] Marcus Lin: We treat them as append-only and restrict access. Also, exported logs are signed as part of the pipeline. We can share details in the security packet.

[12:16] Priya Desai: I’ll want that. We’ve had vendors say “append only” but then they can delete.

[12:21] Marcus Lin: Deletion is restricted and audited. And we can enforce retention policies rather than ad-hoc deletion.

[12:31] Elena Morozova: Can you clarify RBAC scopes for Dedicated. Like, if we have multiple pools, can approvals be limited per pool.

[12:38] Marcus Lin: Yes, permissions are scoped to tenant and can be constrained to resources like pool_id. There are roles like Viewer, Editor, Approver, Operator. And you can separate “edit plan” from “approve stage.”

[12:55] Priya Desai: Do you support two-person approval, like require two distinct approvers.

[13:00] Paula Mendes: We support “N-of-M” approvals at a stage. In v1 it’s usually 1-of-M, but the model supports multiple required approvals. We’re rolling it out incrementally.

[13:12] Tom Wagner: If it’s not day-1, tell us. We just need to know.

[13:16] Paula Mendes: Fair. For initial Dedicated staged rollout beta, expect one approval requirement per stage. Multi-approver is on the roadmap; we can discuss if it’s a blocker.

[13:28] Priya Desai: We can start with single approver as long as it’s our identity and it’s logged.

[13:33] Elena Morozova: Also, we want a clear separation: Redwood can’t approve on our behalf unless break-glass.

[13:40] Marcus Lin: That’s achievable. We can configure RBAC so Redwood roles can execute operational tasks but cannot approve customer-governed rollouts, except via a break-glass workflow.

[13:52] Tom Wagner: And break-glass is audited. Ok.

[13:56] Miguel Santos: Another common question: do we provide a “change ticket” link. Some customers want to attach a Jira ID.

[14:03] Priya Desai: Yes. Can we add a change request ID or ticket reference.

[14:08] Paula Mendes: The rollout plan has metadata fields. You can include an external_change_id. That gets recorded and shows up in the audit events too.

[14:20] Tom Wagner: Perfect.

[14:22] Elena Morozova: I want to go deeper on rollout actions. What is the full set of things that are audited related to rollouts.

[14:29] Kevin Osei: In addition to create/update/delete (delete is rare and controlled), you have: start execution, stage set-weight, stage advance, stage approval requested/granted, abort, auto-hold, auto-rollback if configured, and policy evaluation changes. Also, permission changes for rollout roles are audited.

[14:55] Priya Desai: Permission changes are audited too? Like adding an approver.

[14:58] Marcus Lin: Yes, RBAC admin actions are logged as security events.

[15:03] Tom Wagner: Ok. What about read access? Do you log who viewed.

[15:08] Marcus Lin: We don’t treat reads as audit events by default—too high volume. For privileged resources, we can enable access logs. For most compliance programs, change events are the primary requirement.

[15:22] Priya Desai: That’s fine. We don’t need view logs.

[15:25] Elena Morozova: Capacity and latency: if you are rolling out 25% traffic to a new model, can that saturate the pool and cause queueing.

[15:33] Paula Mendes: It can, which is why we add gates on queue depth, GPU utilization, and timeout rate. Also, we have a headroom policy so you can’t progress if you don’t have enough capacity. And for Dedicated, we’re careful to keep tenant isolation—your pool changes don’t spill over to others.

[15:52] Priya Desai: Ok. And if it saturates, will the system just keep going or pause.

[15:57] Paula Mendes: Pause/hold. The gates should catch it. And if telemetry is lying, we err on pausing rather than continuing.

[16:06] Tom Wagner: “Telemetry lying” is a good phrase. We’ve had that. Do you have monitoring of the gate evaluator itself.

[16:13] Kevin Osei: Yes, there are dashboards and alerts for evaluator lag, query errors, and metrics freshness. That’s internal today, and we can share some of those signals in the console for transparency.

[16:28] Elena Morozova: Is that in the UI.

[16:30] Paula Mendes: In the rollout stage view, we show gate status: pass/fail/inconclusive, plus last evaluation time and window. If inconclusive due to stale metrics, it will say that.

[16:45] Priya Desai: Great.

[16:47] Miguel Santos: Tom, Priya—do you want to see an example of the audit event payloads.

[16:52] Tom Wagner: Yes, even a redacted example would help.

[16:55] Kevin Osei: I don’t have it pasted here, but I can describe. Example: rollout.approval.granted event includes actor_email, actor_role, tenant_id, pool_id, rollout_plan_id, plan_version, stage_id, approval_policy_id, and a comment field. We also include a correlation id you can tie back to API request.

[17:20] Priya Desai: Comment field—nice. So approver can say “approved per change ticket CHG-1234.”

[17:26] Kevin Osei: Exactly.

[17:28] Elena Morozova: What about rollback. Is rollback a separate event.

[17:33] Kevin Osei: Yes. rollback.initiated and rollback.completed, plus whether it was manual or automatic.

[17:42] Tom Wagner: Good.

[17:44] Miguel Santos: We’ll send sample JSON event payloads after the call. In a doc, not in email.

[17:50] Priya Desai: Please.

[17:52] Ben Carter: One more procurement-y question. Can these features be contractually committed. Like audit logs, approval capability.

[17:59] Miguel Santos: Audit logs and RBAC are part of the enterprise offering. For Dedicated staged rollouts specifically, since it’s rolling out, we’ll handle in the SOW / order form as a beta feature if needed. But yes, we can commit to change auditability outcomes.

[18:19] Tom Wagner: Ok.

[18:21] Priya Desai: I also need to ask: do you ever make changes without telling the customer.

[18:26] Miguel Santos: For non-emergency changes, we provide notice. For emergency security patches, we may need to act fast, but we do notify and log.

[18:36] Marcus Lin: And emergency changes are audited and labeled as such.

[18:41] Priya Desai: Ok.

[18:43] Elena Morozova: Slight tangent: when we talk about “model updates,” are you updating the underlying open model without us asking.

[18:50] Miguel Santos: Not if you pin versions. For Dedicated, you can pin a specific model build. Updates happen through a controlled rollout you initiate or approve.

[19:00] Priya Desai: Great.

[19:02] Tom Wagner: What about Redwood runtime updates, like changing your inference engine version.

[19:08] Paula Mendes: That’s a change type too. It can be rolled out using the same staged mechanism. The plan can specify a runtime build. Again, in beta, Redwood operators might create the plan, but you can be the approver.

[19:25] Priya Desai: That’s ideal.

[19:27] Elena Morozova: Ok. Now, can we talk about “who can do what.” Do you have a matrix.

[19:33] Marcus Lin: Yes. We have a RBAC matrix for rollout permissions: rollout.view, rollout.edit, rollout.approve, rollout.abort. We also have scope boundaries: internal operator vs tenant admin. I can send an excerpt.

[19:49] Tom Wagner: Please do.

[19:51] Priya Desai: Abort permission—who can abort.

[19:54] Paula Mendes: Typically, approvers can abort. And Redwood oncall may have abort via break-glass if there’s an incident.

[20:04] Priya Desai: Ok.

[20:06] Elena Morozova: If a rollout is held, can someone override and continue.

[20:10] Paula Mendes: Yes, but it requires explicit manual approval. The UI shows which gate failed and the metrics. You can proceed with override, but that override is audited.

[20:22] Tom Wagner: Good—override should be logged.

[20:25] Kevin Osei: It is.

[20:26] Priya Desai: Do you have alerts for held rollouts.

[20:30] Miguel Santos: There are internal alerts. For customers, we can set up notifications—email or Slack via your channel. And you can poll status via API.

[20:42] Elena Morozova: Ok.

[20:44] Tom Wagner: I want to be clear: this staged rollout capability is important to us, but even without it, we need auditability for any manual changes you make today.

[20:54] Marcus Lin: Understood. Even today, operational actions are logged. The staged rollouts project is adding more granularity and customer-facing workflows, but audit logs exist for admin operations already.

[21:08] Priya Desai: Ok. Do you have an example of an existing event for “pool config changed.”

[21:14] Kevin Osei: Yes. It’s a pool.update event with actor, tenant, pool id, and changed fields. We’ll include both existing and the new rollout-specific events.

[21:26] Elena Morozova: Great.

[21:28] Miguel Santos: Anything else on change management.

[21:31] Priya Desai: One more. Can you enforce that production changes happen only during a change window.

[21:36] Paula Mendes: We can enforce time-based constraints in policy. For example, stage advancement only allowed during a defined window, or require manual approval outside of it. It’s not fully self-serve in v1, but the model supports it.

[21:54] Tom Wagner: Ok.

[21:56] Priya Desai: And approvals: can you require MFA.

[22:00] Marcus Lin: If you use SSO, your MFA policy applies. For API tokens, we recommend limiting usage and using short-lived tokens, but for approvals we recommend console approvals.

[22:14] Elena Morozova: Makes sense.

[22:16] Ben Carter: Just checking: any of this involves additional data being stored. Like, are prompts or outputs stored in audit logs.

[22:24] Kevin Osei: No. Audit logs contain metadata about actions, not content. They include resource IDs and configuration changes, but not customer request payloads.

[22:35] Priya Desai: Great.

[22:37] Tom Wagner: Ok, I think we covered audit logs. Now I want to know how you define a “rollout action.” For example, if you adjust a gate threshold, is that a separate change.

[22:48] Paula Mendes: Yes. Updating gate thresholds is an update to the rollout plan. That emits rollout.update, and if it changes execution behavior it may require re-approval depending on policy.

[23:02] Elena Morozova: So you can’t silently loosen gates.

[23:05] Paula Mendes: Not without an audited update and the right permissions.

[23:10] Priya Desai: Great.

[23:11] Miguel Santos: Maybe we should talk through a concrete scenario.

[23:14] Elena Morozova: Sure. Let’s say we want to upgrade from Model A v1.2 to v1.3. Stage 1 is 5%. Gate on p95 latency and 5xx. After 30 minutes, it passes. Then stage 2 is 25% after approval. How do we approve.

[23:34] Paula Mendes: In console, you’d see the stage “Ready to advance,” with gate summary. Approver clicks Approve & Advance. The system records the approver identity, the stage id, and advances weights deterministically.

[23:49] Kevin Osei: And emits audit event rollout.approval.granted, and stage.advanced.

[23:55] Priya Desai: Ok. And if it fails, auto hold.

[23:58] Paula Mendes: Correct.

[24:00] Tom Wagner: And if it fails but we still want to proceed, there’s an override event.

[24:05] Paula Mendes: Exactly.

[24:07] Elena Morozova: One more question: do you provide API to fetch audit logs.

[24:12] Kevin Osei: There is an API for audit events, with pagination, filtering by time, by resource, by actor. Most customers prefer export, but the API exists.

[24:25] Priya Desai: Great.

[24:27] Tom Wagner: Ok. I’m satisfied.

[24:30] Miguel Santos: Great. Let’s recap what we’ll send: audit event schema examples, retention and export options, RBAC matrix excerpt.

[24:39] Priya Desai: And if you can, include a statement about break-glass and how it’s audited.

[24:44] Marcus Lin: Yes, I’ll include that.

[24:47] Elena Morozova: And Paula, can you share default gate thresholds you recommend for Dedicated.

[24:52] Paula Mendes: Yes, with the caveat they’re tunable by workload, but I’ll share typical defaults.

[24:59] Ben Carter: And pricing for SIEM streaming later.

[25:02] Miguel Santos: Yep, I’ll follow up separately.

[25:05] Priya Desai: Thanks everyone.

[25:07] Miguel Santos: Thank you.

[25:10] (cross-talk)

[25:12] Fireflies.ai note: Transcript continues with informal Q&A; no additional decisions recorded.
